findings.claim: 'around 250,000 Iraqi soldiers dead' in the Iran-Iraq war.
findings.truth: Estimates of Iraqi military deaths range widely, commonly 105,000-200,000, though higher figures circulate. The figure is at the top of the range but not demonstrably wrong, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: Britannica and Wikipedia 'Iran-Iraq War' give wide ranges

findings.claim: The Strait of Hormuz is 'just thirty-three kilometres wide at its narrowest'.
findings.truth: It is 21 nautical miles, about 39 km, at its narrowest. 33 km comes from misreading 21 nautical miles as 21 statute miles.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Strait of Hormuz': minimum width 21 nmi (39 km)

findings.truth: Japan contributed about $13 billion; Germany contributed about $6 billion, not $10 billion.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Coalition of the Gulf War': Japan approximately $13 billion, Germany $6 billion in cash and material

findings.claim: 'President George H. W. Bush was at his Maine summer house in Kennebunkport' when Iraq invaded on 2 August 1990.
findings.truth: Most accounts place Bush in Washington on the morning of 2 August 1990, chairing a National Security Council meeting before flying to Aspen. I could not confirm either version tonight (the fetchable Wikipedia and State Department pages do not cover his movements). Options: (a) delete the Kennebunkport clause and simply say he flew to Aspen that day; (b) verify against the Bush Presidential Library daily diary before editing.
findings.evidence: no fetchable source found; Wikipedia 'Presidency of George H. W. Bush' and history.state.gov are silent

findings.claim: 'Thatcher's line at Aspen, "remember George, this is no time to go wobbly"' - the lesson and a flashcard both tie the remark to the Aspen meeting of 2 August 1990.
findings.truth: Thatcher's own memoir and Charles Powell place the remark in a later telephone call, usually dated 26 August 1990 and about intercepting Iraqi shipping, not at Aspen. I could not verify tonight. Options: (a) keep the quotation but drop 'at Aspen' from both the lesson and the flashcard; (b) verify against the Thatcher Foundation archive and date it properly.
findings.evidence: margaretthatcher.org returned 403; Wikipedia and Wikiquote pages do not carry the line

findings.claim: '35 contributing nations' in the coalition.
findings.truth: Counts vary: the US State Department says 34, Wikipedia says 42. 34-35 is the usual textbook figure, so the claim is defensible and is left alone.
findings.evidence: history.state.gov 'The Gulf War' gives thirty-four countries

findings.claim: 'Coalition combat deaths totalled around 392'; a flashcard adds 'with several hundred more in non-combat incidents'.
findings.truth: 392 is the total coalition military death toll from all causes across every contributing nation. Deaths caused by enemy action were far fewer - US figures alone are 292 dead of whom 147 were killed by enemy action.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Gulf War': 292 killed (147 by enemy action, 145 non-hostile)

findings.claim: 'Around 4,400 American servicemen had been killed in Iraq' by 20 January 2009.
findings.truth: US deaths stood at roughly 4,230 when Bush left office; 4,400-4,500 is the figure for the whole war to 2011. The text says 'around', so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: widely published US casualty counts

findings.claim: 'The 1995 oil-for-food programme'.
findings.truth: UN Resolution 986 was adopted in April 1995 but Iraq only accepted it in 1996 and the first oil was exported in December 1996. '1995' is standard shorthand for the resolution, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: UN Security Council Resolution 986 (1995)

summary: Every lesson carries at least one exam-form error: 44 of the 72 practice questions were set in forms this section does not ask, and five exam tips described the 16-mark essay as source-based, two of them telling students to invent source provenance. Factual errors fixed include the 19th-province date, Lakhdar Brahimi's nationality, Hani Hanjour in the Hamburg cell, the Strait of Hormuz width, Germany's Gulf War contribution, coalition combat deaths, Mavis Leno, and the 61-day Afghan campaign.
